title: US battery startups find a lifeline in defense sector amid EV incentive cuts
summary: US battery startups, facing reduced demand due to the elimination of EV incentives, have turned to the defense sector for growth. The Department of Energy awarded $500 million in grants to bolster the domestic battery supply chain, with much of the funding going to startups like Coreshell, Lilac Solutions, and Nth Cycle. These companies are developing technologies for lithium extraction, battery recycling, and advanced materials, with defense applications ranging from drones to fighter jets. While the automotive industry remains a larger market, defense contracts provide critical support amid uncertain EV adoption timelines.
key_points: The US Department of Energy awarded $500M in grants to strengthen the domestic battery supply chain, focusing on reducing foreign reliance and enhancing national security.
Startups like Coreshell ($50M), Lilac Solutions ($100M), and Nth Cycle ($100M) received significant funding for projects including lithium extraction, battery recycling, and advanced anode materials.
Defense applications (drones, torpedoes, radios, jets) are driving demand for domestically sourced batteries, with the Defense Logistics Agency spending ~$200M annually on batteries.
The automotive industry remains the dominant market (~$18B in US battery manufacturing spending in 2026), but defense contracts provide stability amid EV policy uncertainty.
The shift highlights the Pentagon’s need for lightweight, capable batteries from US sources after EV incentive cuts disrupted domestic production plans.
